cards.front: What is the Neer classification of proximal humerus fractures?
cards.back: Based on number of displaced parts (1-4 parts): 1-part = <1 cm displacement. 2-part = surgical neck or greater tuberosity displaced. 3-part = greater tuberosity + surgical neck. 4-part = both tuberosities + surgical neck displaced. More parts = higher avascular necrosis risk.

cards.front: What is the Garden classification of femoral neck fractures and its clinical significance?
cards.back: Type I: incomplete, valgus impacted (lowest AVN risk). Type II: complete, non-displaced. Type III: complete, partially displaced. Type IV: completely displaced (highest AVN risk). Types I-II = internal fixation; Types III-IV = arthroplasty in elderly.

cards.front: What is the most common nerve injured in a distal humerus fracture?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve — most commonly injured due to its proximity to the medial epicondyle. Always check ulnar nerve function (sensation to small finger, finger abduction/adduction) in distal humerus fractures.

cards.front: What is the Ottawa ankle rule?
cards.back: Clinical decision rule to determine need for X-ray: X-ray indicated if bony tenderness at posterior edge or tip of lateral/medial malleolus OR inability to bear weight (4 steps) immediately after injury and in ED. Sensitivity >95%.
